description: Somos un equipo interesado en la ciencia, la tecnología y la innovación, con habilidades en análisis de datos, programación en Python, sistemas de información geográfica (SIG) y teledetección satelital mediante Google Earth Engine.En el NASA Space Apps Challenge buscamos integrar nuestros conocimientos, aprender nuevas herramientas y transformar datos científicos en propuestas innovadoras que contribuyan a resolver problemas reales y generar un impacto positivo en nuestro entorno.
summary: How do you tell a dry season from a lasting change in the Andes? Ampay Vivo is an interactive geoportal prototype for Ampay National Sanctuary in Apurímac, Peru, where glacial retreat, water deficits, and climate change put a glacier, high-Andean lakes, and native intimpa forest at risk. We bring NASA and Copernicus Earth observation data together in maps and monthly charts covering vegetation, snow cover, temperature, rainfall, and solar radiation. For the “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge, we show how users can compare seasons and investigate whether a pattern persists over time. This gives protected-area managers, researchers, educators, and local communities a shared record for deciding where and when to look more closely.
details:
What is "Ampay Vivo"?

Ampay Vivo is an interactive geoportal prototype for Ampay National Sanctuary in Apurímac, Peru, where glacial retreat, water deficits, and climate change put a glacier, high-Andean lakes, and native intimpa forest at risk.

What users can explore?

Ampay Vivo pairs maps of the study area with monthly time series. A user can start with a question such as “When is Ampay driest?” and look at the rainfall record alongside vegetation moisture, snow cover, and temperature. Looking at the same season across different years helps distinguish the expected wet–dry cycle from a pattern that may persist. Each record carries the source, spatial resolution, observation count, valid coverage, and quality flag so users can assess the evidence behind a chart.

How we built it?

We used JavaScript in Google Earth Engine to process open satellite and climate datasets over a common study boundary, and Python to check and consolidate the exports. Our five modules cover:

•    Vegetation. Sentinel-2 NDVI, SAVI, and EVI describe vegetation greenness or vigor, while NDMI gives an indication of vegetation moisture.

•   Water and cryosphere. Sentinel-2 NDSI and mapped snow-covered area describe surface snow conditions. NDMI adds moisture context. A snow-covered area can include seasonal snow, so a glacier outline or field evidence is needed to quantify glacier retreat independently.

•    Temperature. NASA Terra MODIS provides daytime and nighttime land-surface temperature. ERA5-Land provides air temperature at two meters. The series retain their separate physical meanings and spatial resolutions.

•    Precipitation. CHIRPS v3 and NASA GPM IMERG V07 provide monthly precipitation estimates. We retain a dedicated IMERG series for analysis and track the product used for each month.

•    Solar radiation. ERA5-Land and NASA MODIS estimate incoming shortwave radiation. Where MODIS coverage is missing, the NASA-based series uses the modeled shortwave forcing field from SMAP Level 4.

Who it can help?

Sanctuary managers and researchers can use the record to choose when to inspect snow cover or vegetation conditions in the field. Educators and local groups can use the same maps and charts to see how the wet and dry seasons shape Ampay. Our immediate goal is to make the sanctuary’s environmental record usable by people who would otherwise have to download and process each dataset separately.
